lyrics:
They told me to find what works for me
so I found work at half past eight
A badge, a bell, a numbered key —
same machine that logged my weight

The guitar went quiet in its case
One pen signed a ring, a lease, a loan
Somebody's car, somebody's place —
and every name on it my own

Work is what a man is worth
work is how the man gets made
Mine came first. Mine came from birth
I set it down and made the trade

Some years in, my hands gave out
on a box a man should lift
I called it soft. I called it doubt
Clocked back in for the second shift

Work is what a man is worth
work is how the man gets made
Mine came first. Mine came from birth
I set it down and made the trade

Nobody asked me what it cost
Nobody took it. I handed it over
No one to blame and no one to thank —
I know the hour. I know what I lost

Work is what a man is worth
work is how the man gets made
Mine came first. Mine came from birth
I set it down and made the trade

Still clocking in
Still doesn't work

[Short Instrumental Intro - mechanical, limping 5/4]

[Verse 1 - deadpan, matter-of-fact]

so I found work at half past eight.

[Verse 2 - dry, itemized]

One pen signed a ring, a lease, a loan.

and every name on it my own.

[Chorus - flat, straight time]
Work is what a man is worth,
work is how the man gets made.
Mine came first. Mine came from birth.
I set it down and made the trade.

[Interlude - lone electric guitar, lyrical]

[Verse 3 - quieter, later]
Some years in, my hands gave out
on a box a man should lift.
I called it soft. I called it doubt.
Clocked back in for the second shift.

[Chorus - flat, straight time]
Work is what a man is worth,
work is how the man gets made.
Mine came first. Mine came from birth.
I set it down and made the trade.

[Bridge - stripped, plain]
Nobody asked me what it cost.
Nobody took it. I handed it over.
No one to blame and no one to thank —
I know the hour. I know what I lost.

[Final Chorus - fuller, harmonized]
Work is what a man is worth,
work is how the man gets made.
Mine came first. Mine came from birth.
I set it down and made the trade.

[Outro - thinning, unresolved]
Still clocking in.
Still doesn't work.

[End]
style: Male baritone, resonant, dry deadpan delivery, Progressive rock, Canterbury scene, 116 BPM, mechanical Rhodes-and-clavinet ostinato, limping odd meter into straight-time chorus, bass clarinet, one lyrical electric guitar solo, Warm live-ensemble production, unhurried workmanlike groove

  Approved critic summary: Rose builds this one on a 3/4 pulse at a brisk clip, which is the first surprise: a waltz that never asks you to sway, driven instead by a Hammond groove and gritty guitar working against the meter rather than settling into it.

  Approved critic summary: Michael Anthony Rose’s *Wazoo in Effigy* is inspired by Frank Zappa, which is not quite the same thing as being a Zappa tribute.

The track runs 3:29 in F# major, built on dry, close-miked fingerpicking and a baritone vocal that has the stillness of someone writing in the early morning before anyone else is awake.

impression.text: This track establishes a vibrant, nostalgic pop-rock atmosphere that feels simultaneously uplifting and emotionally driven. The energy remains consistently high throughout the song, propelled by a driving rhythm section of punchy drums, a lively electric bassline, and bright piano accents. The production is densely layered and highly polished, allowing the commanding lead and rich backing vocals to sit clearly above a wide wall of instrumentation. A defining characteristic of the arrangement is the soaring electric guitar solo that bursts into the mix midway through, injecting a surge of melodic intensity before seamlessly transitioning back into the anthemic chorus.

review.review_text: The trick here is baked into the meter: a limping intro before the chorus snaps into flat, straight 4/4 at a workmanlike 117 BPM, the arrangement enacting the very grind the lyrics describe. Rose's deadpan baritone itemizes a life traded away without complaint, and the writing lands because it refuses drama: "One pen signed a ring, a lease, a loan / Somebody's car, somebody's place, and every name on it my own." The lone electric solo midway is the one place the guitar gets to sing before clocking back in, a small mercy that pays off the caged "guitar went quiet in its case" line. It ends unresolved, "Still clocking in / Still doesn't work," and the flatness that keeps this from being a knockout is also the whole point; a grower that rewards the second listen, worthy of your time.
